outputs.L3:
The passage presents fear as something that emerges when the ordinary world becomes unfamiliar. Spaces and objects that should feel safe or recognizable suddenly appear strange, unreal, or even threatening. This produces an intense sense of unease: the speaker is not simply afraid of an external danger, but of the possibility that the world itself has changed in some disturbing way. Familiar surroundings no longer offer comfort, and the boundary between the known and the unknown begins to collapse.

Images of decay play an important role in creating this atmosphere of instability and dread. Rotten window frames, blistering paint, and crumbling buildings suggest that the physical environment is deteriorating. These details make the setting feel unsafe, as though it can no longer be trusted to protect or contain the speaker. Decay also implies the passage of time, neglect, and hidden corruption. What once may have seemed solid and familiar has become fragile and threatening, mirroring the speaker’s own anxious state of mind.

The text also repeatedly points to anxieties about recognition and identity. There is a fear of returning to a place after time has passed and finding that it no longer feels like home. This creates a deeper emotional disturbance: if familiar places have become strange, then the speaker’s own sense of self may also be uncertain. The inability to feel at home suggests displacement, alienation, and a loss of connection to the past. Recognition becomes unreliable, and the speaker is left questioning both the world and their place within it.

Supernatural and uncanny details intensify this mood of terror. The appearance of white wolves, windows that open by themselves, and a crudely drawn eye introduce elements that seem irrational or impossible. These images make the environment feel watched, haunted, or animated by some unknown force. The eye in particular suggests surveillance and vulnerability, as though the speaker is exposed to a gaze they cannot understand or escape. Such details heighten the sense that reality has become unstable and that ordinary explanations are no longer sufficient.

Finally, the fragmented references to specific phobias emphasize a mind overwhelmed by fear. Rather than presenting one clear source of terror, the text accumulates many forms of dread: misgiving, bodily panic, fear of the unfamiliar, fear of decay, and fear that reality itself may be no more than a dream. This fragmentation reflects the speaker’s mental state, suggesting confusion and psychological pressure. The result is a powerful atmosphere of uncanny anxiety, in which the speaker is trapped between waking and dreaming, recognition and estrangement, safety and threat.
outputs.L4:
The text explores uncanny fear, estrangement, and domestic horror through a fragmented collage of gothic images, parenthetical phobia-like definitions, and disjointed first-person perceptions. Rather than presenting terror as a single, identifiable event, it builds an atmosphere of unease through accumulation: strange rooms, distorted bodies, unstable voices, and ordinary objects that seem to have become subtly hostile. The familiar world is not destroyed, but altered just enough to feel wrong. Home, language, memory, and the body cease to offer comfort or certainty, becoming instead sites of anxiety and suspicion.

A major feature of the text is its use of fragmentation. The broken structure mirrors the speaker’s unsettled state of mind, suggesting that fear has disrupted not only the surrounding world but also the ability to describe it coherently. Images appear and vanish without clear explanation, creating a sense of disorientation. This lack of narrative stability makes the reader share in the speaker’s uncertainty: it is never fully clear whether the horror is external, psychological, remembered, imagined, or some combination of all of these.

The parenthetical definitions intensify this effect by giving fear a clinical or catalogued quality. They resemble entries from a list of phobias, as if the speaker is trying to classify terror in order to control it. Yet these definitions do not resolve the fear; instead, they multiply it. By naming anxieties so precisely, the text suggests that dread can attach itself to almost anything: rooms, faces, mouths, silence, darkness, touch, or even words themselves. Language becomes both a tool of explanation and a source of further estrangement.

Domestic space is especially important. The horror does not come from a distant wilderness or an obvious supernatural monster, but from spaces that should be safe and intimate. Rooms, corridors, furniture, and familiar household details become uncanny because they are recognizable and alien at the same time. This is the central gothic tension of the piece: the home is no longer a refuge but a place where hidden fears surface. The ordinary is made monstrous through perception.

The body is treated in a similar way. Instead of appearing stable or reassuring, bodies are fragmented, watched, or distorted. Faces, limbs, skin, and voices may seem detached from identity, turning human presence into something strange and threatening. The first-person perspective heightens this instability because the speaker’s perceptions cannot be fully trusted. The reader is placed inside a consciousness that is intensely aware, but not necessarily able to interpret what it sees.

The key effect of the text is therefore to make familiar spaces, bodies, and words feel alien and dangerous. Its horror does not depend on a clear external monster or a conventional plot of pursuit and attack. Instead, terror arises from perception itself: from the possibility that the world has not changed, but the speaker’s relation to it has. The text suggests that fear can emerge when recognition fails, when language breaks down, and when the ordinary becomes impossible to inhabit safely. In this way, it creates a powerful sense of uncanny dread, showing how horror can exist not outside the self, but in the act of seeing, naming, and remembering.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a five-part experimental prose collage using fragments of Gothic literature, domestic horror imagery, and parenthetical phobia definitions; make it disjointed, uncanny, and numbered.
counterfactuals.output:
1. **THE HALLWAY**

The house had been waiting with its mouth open.

A candle guttered in the corridor, though no one had lit it. The wallpaper—yellowed, damp, patterned with little thorned vines—seemed to creep when I looked away. Somewhere behind the nursery door, a music box played three notes and forgot the fourth.

Mother said: *Do not answer the knocking from inside the walls.*

(Achluophobia: fear of darkness.)

At midnight, the portraits turned their faces toward the kitchen, where the sink overflowed with black water and baby teeth.

I found a note beneath my pillow in a handwriting I had used as a child:

**THE CELLAR IS HUNGRY AGAIN.**


2. **THE CRADLE**

Rock, rock.

The cradle moved by itself, though the infant had been buried in March.

Rock, rock.

In the parlor, lace curtains breathed against the glass. In the pantry, flour spilled in a perfect circle. Father’s boots stood by the fire, full of rainwater and moths.

(Pedophobia: fear of children or dolls.)

The doll on the mantel had my grandmother’s eyes, my sister’s ribbon, my own small cracked mouth. When I held it to my ear, I heard a woman whispering from very far away:

*I was promised a daughter.*

The cradle stopped.

The house listened.


3. **THE CUPBOARD UNDER THE STAIRS**

There are places in a home not built for living.

Behind the broom, behind the chipped enamel bucket, behind the smell of vinegar and old wool, a little door appeared. It had no knob. It had a keyhole shaped like an open eye.

(Claustrophobia: fear of enclosed spaces.)

I bent down.

The keyhole blinked.

From within came the sound of dinner being served: knives laid neatly beside plates, spoons chiming, chairs scraping backward for guests who had not survived the winter. Someone laughed with a throat full of dust.

The roast was gray.

The hymn was wrong.

The family ate in silence, wearing my face.


4. **THE BEDROOM MIRROR**

No mirror in the house reflected the same room twice.

In the oval glass above the vanity, I saw a chamber hung with velvet. In the cracked mirror by the wardrobe, a narrow bed soaked in rain. In the silver hand mirror, only a staircase descending forever into candlelight.

(Spectrophobia: fear of mirrors or one’s reflection.)

At dawn, my reflection remained asleep while I stood awake.

At noon, it sat up.

By evening, it pressed its palms to the glass and mouthed the words:

*Let me wear you.*

I covered the mirror with a sheet.

All night, from beneath the linen, someone practiced my smile.


5. **THE RETURN**

The front door opened onto the front door.

Beyond it: the same hallway, the same candle, the same portraits pretending innocence. The floorboards sighed under my feet like old servants remembering orders.

(Oikophobia: fear of home or household surroundings.)

I ran through room after room: nursery, parlor, pantry, bedroom, stair. Each chamber folded into the next like damp paper. Each window showed not the garden, but another room. Each room contained a woman standing with her back turned.

At last I reached the kitchen.

The sink was dry.

The cradle was still.

The cupboard door was open.

On the table lay a place setting for one, a black napkin, and a note:

**WELCOME HOME.**

Then the house closed its mouth.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

**INDEX OF SMALL WRONGNESS, FOUND IN THE KITCHEN DRAWER**

A.  
The house exhales at 3:17 a.m. through the vents. Not a sigh. A practice breath.  
(The fear of air becoming an animal.)  
Someone has moved the spoons into the sock drawer again, nested bowl-up, shining like fish eyes.

B.  
Baby monitor: static, then a voice saying *don’t turn around, I’m almost you*.  
There is no baby.  
There is, however, a cradle in the pantry full of receipt paper and fingernail clippings.

C.  
(The fear of strangers knowing which key is yours.)  
A man at the door asks if this is where he lives. He has your father’s coat, your dentist’s teeth, your signature written on the back of his hand.  
You say no.  
He nods like you have passed the first test.

D.  
Cupboard, lower left: the plates are warm.  
Cupboard, lower right: one plate missing, replaced by a photograph of the hallway taken from inside the wall.

E.  
Monster, under bed — see also: husband.  
Monster, in mirror — see also: childhood photographs.  
Monster, making tea — see also: mother, possibly.

F.  
(The fear of being recognized incorrectly.)  
At the supermarket, a woman embraces you and weeps into your neck.  
“I thought you were dead,” she says.  
You want to tell her she has the wrong person, but her grief fits too well.

G.  
Narrative fragment, charred at edges:  
*We were eating dinner when the basement coughed. Everyone pretended not to hear it. The peas rolled clockwise on their own plates. Father said grace twice, once in English, once in the language he only speaks when asleep.*

H.  
Hair in the bathtub drain: too long to be yours, too short to be a stranger’s.  
(The fear of evidence without event.)

I.  
There is a silhouette in the laundry room wearing all your missing socks over its hands. It bends politely. It has no face, only a folded napkin where the face should be.  
You close the door.  
It knocks from the inside using your knuckles.

J.  
Known issue: sometimes the family portrait rearranges itself by hunger.  
Known issue: sometimes “family” includes additional figures in the back row, damp from rain, smiling with borrowed mouths.

K.  
(The fear of the beloved being replaced by something patient.)  
Your sister calls and says, “I’m outside.”  
Your sister has been asleep in the guest room for eleven years.  
Outside, someone waves with her left hand.  
Inside, someone waves back with her right.

L.  
Lamp flicker. Meat smell. Wallpaper pulse.  
A dog barking from the oven.  
A child laughing in the freezer.  
Your name whispered from the clean laundry, folded into every shirt.

M.  
Misrecognition, common forms:  
1. Mistaking a shadow for a person.  
2. Mistaking a person for a shadow.  
3. Mistaking yourself for the one who came home.  
4. Mistaking home for a place that wants you.

N.  
(The fear of doors remembering hands.)  
Each knob in the house has become slightly warm, as if recently gripped.  
The front door opens inward now.  
So does the back door.  
So do the walls.

O.  
Fragment recovered from under the sink:  
*The stranger sat with us at breakfast. No one objected because he had Mother’s laugh. He buttered toast with a knife that reflected all of us except me. When I asked his name, he said, “You already gave it to me.”*

P.  
Pantry inventory:  
- flour, weeping  
- sugar, gray  
- rice, moving subtly toward the door  
- one jar labeled **TEETH / DO NOT RETURN**  
- one jar labeled **THE FEAR OF BEING STORED**

Q.  
Questionnaire for visitors:  
Do you know me?  
Have you always known me?  
If I remove my face, will you still insist?  
When you say “welcome back,” where do you think I have been?

R.  
(The fear of monsters with good manners.)  
It wipes its feet before entering.  
It compliments the curtains.  
It asks after your health.  
Its shadow arrives fifteen minutes later carrying flowers.

S.  
Sink full of black water.  
In the reflection: a ceiling fan, though there is no ceiling fan.  
In the reflection: a hand on your shoulder, though there is no hand.  
In the reflection: you, but relieved to see someone else.

T.  
Telephone message, saved, unsent, repeating:  
“Hi. It’s me. I’m in the house. I mean I’m outside the house. I mean the house is inside me. Please don’t let me answer the door.”

U.  
(The fear of becoming anecdotal.)  
They will say: she was always nervous.  
They will say: the house was old.  
They will say: grief does strange things.  
They will say this while stepping over the claw marks in the breakfast nook.

V.  
Visitor protocol:  
If the stranger resembles a dead relative, offer water.  
If the stranger resembles yourself, do not speak first.  
If the stranger resembles no one, check the mirrors.  
If the stranger has no reflection, check yours.

W.  
At night, the refrigerator hums the tune your grandmother used to hum before she forgot language.  
Inside: a bowl of milk, a single black feather, three eggs cracked neatly from within.  
(The fear of nourishment having intentions.)

X.  
X-ray of the home reveals:  
- ribs in the staircase  
- a second staircase beneath the first  
- a small room behind your bedroom wall where someone has been practicing your handwriting  
- teeth in the chimney  
- a heart, not located centrally

Y.  
You wake to find the word **MOTHER** written in steam on the bathroom mirror.  
You live alone.  
You have never called anyone mother.  
Behind you, the shower curtain breathes.

Z.  
(The fear of the index ending before the thing is named.)  
Final note, overwritten many times:  
*It is not the monster that frightens me. It is the moment the monster looks confused and says my name tenderly. It is the stranger at the table asking why I’m late. It is the mirror refusing to accuse me. It is the house, patient and domestic, setting one more place.*

counterfactuals.output:
1. **Leukophobia — fear of the color white**

“Do not follow the rabbit past the pantry door.”

The old house exhales flour dust, moth powder, bone ash.  
Every room is sheeted in white: white curtains, white bowls,  
a white dog asleep beneath the piano with its eyes open.

In the dream, my teeth are small stones in a glass of milk.  
Someone upstairs is unwrapping bandages from a mirror.  
Someone downstairs is boiling lace.

I press my ear to the wall and hear my blood  
moving like wet mice through plaster.

2. **Oikophobia — fear of the home**

“The staircase remembers every foot but mine.”

At night the house grows extra rooms—  
a nursery full of dead flies,  
a bathroom tiled with fingernails,  
a bedroom where the bed is breathing.

The wallpaper peels in long yellow tongues.  
Behind it: damp horsehair, black mold, a photograph  
of a family with their faces scratched into moons.

A white cat sits in the hall, too still to be alive.  
When I touch it, it collapses into dust  
and a child laughs from the chimney.

3. **Somniphobia — fear of sleep**

“I woke with soil in my mouth again.”

In the dream I am buried upright in the garden,  
my hands blooming above me like pale roots.  
A white deer lowers its head to graze  
on the skin of my wrists.

The doctor writes: nocturnal panic, tactile hallucination,  
possible dissociation from the body.

But the sheets are full of beetle shells.  
But the pillow smells of cellar water.  
But there is a handprint on my chest  
from the inside.

4. **Thanatophobia — fear of death**

“Mother kept the dead canary in the sugar tin.”

The kitchen sags into rot and sweetness.  
Pears liquefy in a blue bowl.  
A lamb stands in the doorway, immaculate,  
with flies stitching its mouth shut.

My pulse is a spoon tapping porcelain.  
My tongue has learned the taste of pennies.  
Under the floorboards, something soft is turning over,  
patient as a buried illness.

The house does not creak.  
It chews.

5. **Mysophobia — fear of contamination**

“Wash until the water admits what it knows.”

I scrub my hands in the clawfoot tub  
while snow falls upward past the window.  
The soap is gray. The water thickens.  
A white snake coils in the drain  
and whispers my childhood name.

There is mold in the shape of lungs on the ceiling.  
There is a door in the mirror, swollen shut.  
There is a bruise spreading beneath my skin  
like ink dropped into cream.

The doctor says: intrusive thoughts, compulsive cleansing.  
The house says: open your mouth.  
The body says nothing,  
but something inside it knocks.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

**Five Years in the House That Would Not Learn My Name**

After five years, the hallway still turns its shoulder to me.  
The key enters like a splinter. The door sighs in the old language of hinges,  
and the rooms remain arranged around an absence  
I have been asked to inhabit.

On the table:  
one cracked thimble, three black cherries, a letter opener shaped like a stork,  
a prescription bottle full of teeth,  
a map with every river crossed out,  
my gloves damp from no weather.

The mirror repeats: *pulse, pupil, pressure.*  
The mirror repeats: *pulse, pupil, pressure.*  
The mirror repeats: *Are you experiencing dizziness, dread, discharge, disappearance?*

In the bedroom, the wallpaper blooms with bruises.  
The bed is a narrow coffin trained to look domestic.  
Some nights the ceiling lowers itself by inches,  
as if measuring me for a family vault  
(fear of ceilings becoming intimate).  
I sleep with one hand outside the blanket  
to prove I am not buried.

Five years, and the stairs still count me incorrectly.  
Five years, and the cupboard keeps a place set for someone thinner.  
Five years, and the windows show only the garden at midnight:  
foxglove, yew, a shovel leaning against the moon,  
the roses opening their red medical mouths.

Take one tablet before memory.  
Take one tablet after the sound in the walls.  
Take one tablet if the house calls you by your childhood nickname.  
Do not exceed the recommended dosage of belonging.

I have hung my coat on every hook.  
I have left hair in the drain, salt in the corners,  
receipts, needles, orange peels, a spoon bent backward,  
a photograph of no one I recognize.  
Still the rooms refuse evidence.  
Still the dust gathers into small juries.

At dinner, the chandelier trembles with ancestral insects.  
The plates are cold and formal.  
The soup tastes faintly of churchyard rain  
(fear of being nourished by the wrong century).  
A chair scrapes itself closer when I am not looking.

My bloodwork returns: inconclusive.  
My bloodwork returns: a flock of ravens.  
My bloodwork returns: please verify your address.

Dear Doctor, the ache is not located in the body.  
Dear Doctor, the body is located in the ache.  
Dear Doctor, when I press here, the room winces.

In the attic: a doll’s arm, a tarnished bell,  
seven dead moths folded like telegrams,  
a trunk full of women’s names scratched into soap.  
I add mine. It dissolves by morning.

And beneath the floorboards—  
not a heart, not exactly,  
but something keeping time badly.  
Something damp and velvet.  
Something that whispers *tenant, tenant, tenant*  
(fear of being mistaken for the temporary dead).

Five years, I say to the mantel.  
Five years, I say to the locked nursery.  
Five years, I say to the black dress moving by itself in the wardrobe.  
The house answers with its mouth full of nails.

Outside, the road remembers leaving.  
Inside, the candles bend away from me.  
I have learned the rituals:  
bleed the radiators, bless the threshold,  
ignore the portrait whose eyes are new each morning.  
Yet every room remains a waiting room.

Name. Date of birth. Symptom.  
Name. Date of birth. Symptom.  
Name: not here.  
Date of birth: unfinished.  
Symptom: I keep arriving and arriving  
and no one opens.
